item.title: Multi-Step Underwater Acoustic Channel Prediction via Dual-Domain Structure Preservation and Pretrained Transformer
item.description: arXiv:2611.14592v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Accurate future channel state information (CSI) is essential for underwater acoustic (UWA) communication because delays associated with signal propagation, feedback, scheduling, and transceiver reconfiguration can render currently available CSI outdated. However, most existing predictors estimate only the next channel state and obtain multi-step forecasts through recursive rollout, which causes prediction errors to accumulate as the multipath structure evolves. The scarcity of sea-trial measurements further limits reliable model training. To address these challenges, we propose LLM4UACP, a dual-domain, structure-preserving framework that adapts a pretrained Transformer for few-shot multi-step UWA channel prediction. LLM4UACP extracts complementary features from the channel impulse response (CIR) and channel frequency response (CFR), aligns them through Fourier-consistent fusion, and encodes the fused representation as delay-time tokens. A pretrained Transformer with a frozen backbone is adapted through Butterfly Orthogonal Fine-tuning to jointly predict multiple future CIRs in a single forward pass, thereby avoiding the error accumulation associated with recursive prediction. Experiments on the measured SO-06 and SO-07 channels show that LLM4UACP achieves normalized mean squared error (NMSE) values of 0.0411 and 0.0399, corresponding to reductions of 88.53% and 85.15%, respectively, relative to the most recent baseline. With only 0.11M trainable parameters, LLM4UACP maintains robust performance across varying prediction horizons and observation-window lengths, limited-data settings, and cross-dataset transfer scenarios.
item.dc:creator: Mingjie Cao, Gewei Zhang, Deqing Wang, Lizhao You, Fei-Yun Wu, Liqun Fu

item.title: Evaluating AI Musical Creativity: Towards a Quantitative Multi-Dimensional Framework Based on Value, Novelty, and Surprise
item.description: arXiv:2611.14634v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Despite the increasing sophistication of generative Artificial Intelligence (AI), research on the evaluation of AI-generated musical creativity remains limited. To address this gap, this paper proposes a quantitative framework for the formalization and evaluation of AI musical creativity. Building on Margaret Boden's theory, which conceptualizes creativity in terms of value, novelty, and surprise, the framework adapts and operationalizes these three dimensions for the musical domain. On the hypothesis that certain aspects of musical creativity can be assessed with a degree of objectivity, a domain-specific set of quantitative metrics for evaluating the creativity of AI-generated music is introduced. Rather than reducing musical creativity to a single unifying measure, this article proposes an ensemble of complementary metrics that capture its different dimensions, recognizing the complexity of musical artifacts and the difficulty of defining meaningful multi-objective compositional criteria. The framework has two implications. First, it gives researchers and developers a principled methodology and quantitative tools for empirically evaluating creative outputs, enabling more informed model development and reducing unnecessary computational costs. Second, it lays the groundwork for future generative models to optimize directly for creativity by adopting these metrics as learning objectives.
item.dc:creator: Hindy Rossignol, Giorgio Franceschelli, Mirco Musolesi

item.title: Harmony: Bridging Audio Understanding and Editing through Agentic Collaboration
item.description: arXiv:2611.14724v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Natural-language audio editing requires connecting a user's intent to specific sounds and time regions while preserving surrounding content. Complex requests make this connection demanding: an edit may select one occurrence, depend on a temporal relation, or modify a source that overlaps with other sounds. We introduce Harmony, an agentic framework that bridges audio understanding and editing through collaboration among an LLM planner, an audio-language model, and external tools. Harmony combines two mechanisms. Edit-driven collaborative planning uses targeted questions and tool measurements to determine the target, timing, and operation parameters. Evidence-guided execution uses observations of the first separated or generated audio to trigger bounded corrections before final mixing. Together, these mechanisms connect semantic decisions to waveform operations throughout the editing process. Harmony supports addition, removal, replacement, and volume adjustment. On 420 MMAE examples spanning these operations, Harmony achieves an exact match rate of 22.62%, compared with 13.57% for the strongest baseline, and improves aggregate instruction following and context preservation.
item.dc:creator: Zhongyi Tong, Yapeng Tian

item.title: Can Music Generation Models Tap Along? Evaluating Generative Approaches to Beat Tracking
item.description: arXiv:2611.14971v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Existing studies have shown that music generative models can generate synchronized tracks that play alongside an input song. Can we extend this capability to develop a generative approach to beat tracking? To answer this question, we equip a pretrained MusicGen model with an audio-conditioning adapter to generate percussion tracks synchronized with the input music, from which we extract the beat positions. We train separate models with percussion targets of varying rhythmic complexity and compare them with two other generative models and conventional beat trackers. On GTZAN, our model achieves performance close to state-of-the-art beat trackers. Our model also demonstrates greater robustness: it shows the smallest drop in F-measure when drums are removed from the input at inference time. In certain genres, such as metal and disco, our model is also less likely to be misled by strong onsets or to miss beats with weak onsets. These results suggest that percussion generation has the potential to become a viable approach to beat tracking, and that its output is not merely a sequence of beat positions but an audible percussion track.
item.dc:creator: Kun Fang, Ziyu Wang, Ichiro Fujinaga

item.title: CFGComposer: Compositional Audio-Text-to-Motion Generation via Copula Score Correction
item.description: arXiv:2611.15101v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Generating whole-body gestures that are simultaneously rhythmically synchronized with speech audio and semantically aligned with text descriptions is a fundamental challenge in embodied AI and social robotics. We tackle this Audio-Text-to-Motion (AT2M) problem by composing two independently-trained diffusion models at inference time and refine bias in joint inference by modeling the copula score $s_I$. A rigorous theoretical analysis reveals that naive epsilon blending corresponds to a Product-of-Experts formulation that omits the copula score $s_I$: the cross-modal interaction between audio and text that neither marginal model can capture. We propose CFGComposer: a jointly-trained AT2M diffusion model that estimates $s_I$ via a CFG analogy and injects it as an $\epsilon$-space correction. Experiments on BEAT demonstrate best-in-class semantic fidelity (SRGR $0.9916$, FID $27.18$) with GT-level beat alignment (BA $0.1826$ vs. GT $0.1743$), and 76-83% win rate in blind pairwise human evaluation against all prior methods. Physical deployment on a Unitree G1 humanoid confirms direct sim-to-real transfer.
item.dc:creator: Pengyang Shi, Jinlu Zhang, Chunze Lin, Yizhou Wang, Li Yi

item.title: Computational Raga Recognition: A Theory-Driven Approach
item.description: arXiv:2611.15242v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Raga recognition in Hindustani classical music is difficult because a raga is not defined only by the notes used in it. Its identity also depends on the way notes are emphasized, the movement between notes and characteristic phrases. In this work, we develop a computational approach to analyse these characteristics directly from audio recordings. The method uses pitch extracted from recordings and represents it using a 44-position note framework based on the 22-shruti system. From this representation, Raga features based on the Indian classical musicology are extracted.Each feature is compared with a reference representation of the raga and the resulting scores are combined to obtain an overall similarity score. The method is first studied using Raga Yaman and is then tested on recordings of other ragas. The computational results are also compared with the theoretical description of Yaman to identify which raga characteristics are captured well and where the method has limitations.
item.dc:creator: Janay Sukheja, Shailaja D. Sharma

item.title: FineSpeaker: Reliable Speaker Representation Learning at Fine Temporal Resolution
item.description: arXiv:2611.15288v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Speaker representation learning is fundamental to speech processing tasks such as speaker verification and diarization. Although long-context speaker encoders can produce stable and discriminative embeddings, short-duration verification and diarization require finer-grained temporal representations. Short temporal contexts limit the available speaker evidence and make speaker identity difficult to disentangle from phonetic and acoustic variability. This creates a temporal resolution-representation reliability trade-off: speaker representations should maintain local within-speaker consistency, between-speaker discriminability and remain sensitive to speaker changes at fine temporal resolution. Accordingly, we propose a framework for reliable speaker representation learning at fine temporal resolution. FineSpeaker first constructs resolution-controllable frame-wise speaker representations through mean pooling over an adjustable n-frame window, enabling flexible control of representation granularity. It then introduces a speaker encoder with local temporal modeling that exploits short-range speaker context to improve the stability and discriminability of short-duration and frame-wise representations. Furthermore, we develop a generative disentanglement strategy for optimizing frame-level speaker representations, combining VAE-based probabilistic modeling with flow matching to characterize speaker-related variation and suppress non-speaker interference. Experiments demonstrate competitive full-utterance performance, improved fine-grained speaker verification on VoxCeleb and CN-Celeb, and strong zero-shot diarization results, highlighting the benefits of balancing temporal resolution and representation reliability.
item.dc:creator: Yongkang Yin, Wenhao Yang, Lichun Fan, Jian Luan, Hang Su, Yuexian Zou

item.title: DeALR: Decoupled Audio-Latent Optimization with Acoustic Backtracking for Test-Time Reasoning
item.description: arXiv:2611.15439v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large audio-language models (LALMs) typically encode audio once and conduct subsequent multi-step reasoning in a language-dominated space, weakening access to fine-grained acoustic evidence. Although recent multimodal approaches have explored re-engaging perceptual inputs during reasoning, whether a frozen LALM can actively revisit crucial acoustic evidence in the latent space at test time remains underexplored. To bridge this gap, we introduce Decoupled Audio Latent Reasoning (DeALR), a novel test-time latent reasoning framework that shifts the paradigm from text-dominated deliberation to active audio-latent interaction. Inspired by the human cognitive process of "backtracking" to specific acoustic cues during complex listening tasks, DeALR establishes a dynamic interaction between learnable thought tokens and acoustic segments. Specifically, we introduce Span-Level Acoustic Backtracking, which traces initial attention distributions to dynamically isolate contiguous, key acoustic spans. Furthermore, we propose Decoupled Audio-Latent Optimization (DALO), a test-time reinforcement learning algorithm that jointly refines thought vectors and acoustic patches via confidence-guided policy gradients. Crucially, DALO explicitly decouples trajectory search from response generation by reinstating uncorrupted, high-fidelity audio embeddings prior to text synthesis, entirely eliminating optimization-induced distribution drift while retaining the navigation of the refined thoughts. Comprehensive experiments on benchmarks demonstrate that DeALR consistently outperforms prior test-time optimization approaches, delivering substantial improvements in both confidence calibration and reasoning accuracy.
item.dc:creator: Haoyu He, Yan Rong, Li Liu

item.title: Right Answers, Inconsistent Evidence: Source-Level Counterfactual Auditing of Large Audio-Language Models
item.description: arXiv:2611.15463v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A large audio-language model (LALM) can answer "is a cat present?" about a mixture correctly, and its confidence can drop when the cat is removed, yet this does not show that it can tell the cat's presence from its absence. We introduce TRACE. It deletes the queried source and each rival in turn and asks whether every view still containing that sound outscores the view with it removed. Across 8 LALMs and 3,456 controlled mixtures, 6.3% of correct answers fail this ordering: the target-absent view scores at or above some target-present view, a conflict no shared threshold repairs. A target-only score check misses 42.5% of them. The share rises from 4.9% to 8.4% as target SNR falls from +5 to -5 dB, even on units correct at every level, and survives loudness and re-pairing controls. Accuracy certifies the answer; TRACE audits whether it orders presence above absence. Code and data: https://github.com/yikise/TRACE.
item.dc:creator: Yi Zhang, Yi Li, Hongwei Du

item.title: RSE-TTS: Compact Text-to-Speech through Shared Text-Aware Reference Encoding and Generation
item.description: arXiv:2611.15464v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Can a speech generator also serve as an effective voice encoder? We show that a pretrained autoregressive text-to-speech (TTS) backbone can be repurposed for reference compression, improving speaker similarity in subsequent synthesis. Jointly encoding reference speech and its transcript further strengthens this capability. Controlled ablations and activation interventions trace the text benefit through intermediate acoustic representations into the compressed vectors that condition generation. Building on these findings, we introduce RSE-TTS, whose Reconstructive Speaker Encoder (RSE) shares the generation backbone and compresses paired reference text and speech into eight continuous vectors. Sharing reduces encoder-generator parameters by 48% relative to independent pretrained encoding. Large-scale English training yields a 118M-parameter generator that improves both word error rate and speaker similarity over the corresponding official MOSS-TTS-Nano cloning modes on all three English benchmarks. Combined with acoustic continuation, RSE-TTS approaches the speaker similarity of substantially larger systems while achieving lower WER than the evaluated CosyVoice 3 and MOSS-TTS-Local models. Audio samples are available at https://voxnexusai.github.io/RSE-TTS/.
item.dc:creator: Ming Ma, Mingjie Chen, Yuanzhong Zheng, Hengyao Bao, Hailin Yu, Shijing Yu, Hao Qiu, Gongfan Cao, Xiao Li, Xuemin Zhao, Youhai Jiang

item.title: On-Edge Acoustic Continual Anomaly Detection: A Cross-Platform Comparative Study
item.description: arXiv:2611.15465v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Acoustic Anomaly Detection (AAD) serves as a non-contact approach for machine condition monitoring, yet much of the existing research is evaluated offline and rarely addresses embedded hardware constraints or microphone variations under operational drift. This paper presents a comparative evaluation of on-edge continual AAD across two embedded platforms the ESP32-S3 (with an external I2S digital microphone) and the Arduino Nicla Vision (with an onboard Pulse Density Modulation (PDM) microphone) using a shared detection model. The model utilizes a lightweight ShallowNet encoder and contrastive prototype learning to map spectrograms into a 32-dimensional embedding space. Both boards run an identical TensorFlow Lite for Microcontrollers (TFLM) encoder, performing on-device prototype learning updated via an exponential moving average. A cloud pipeline orchestrated through Firebase and MQTT enables remote data collection and retraining. Evaluated via a controlled speaker-replay protocol using standardized Detection and Classification of Acoustic Scenes and Events (DCASE) Challenge Task 2 machine sounds, the ESP32-S3 achieved 82.35% to 95.00% accuracy across five machine types, while the Nicla Vision achieved 79.41% to 95.00%. The two platforms demonstrated comparable performance, confirming that the lightweight prototypical architecture transfers reliably across distinct hardware and sensor tiers.
item.dc:creator: Rami Zewail, Yehia Ehab, Karim Ali, Ahmed Mahrous, Mohamed Awad, Bassem Mokhtar

item.title: ZONOS3-Mini Technical Report
item.description: arXiv:2611.16525v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: ZONOS3-Mini is an ultra-compact, ultra-fast, zero-shot voice-cloning TTS model. The model can run in real time on a laptop or smartphone. For its latency and size, it achieves state-of-the-art accuracy and cloning fidelity. To achieve this we propose a latent MoE backbone with only 886M parameters (100M active per token) and a new audio codec, Zyphra Audio Codec 1 (ZAC-1), which represents 44.1 kHz audio at a 15 Hz frame rate. On the new ZTTS2-Eval benchmark, ZONOS3-Mini reaches a 6.71% macro-average WER over 55 language sets (35 clean and 20 in the wild), which is competitive with larger and slower state-of-the-art models. We release the model weights, inference, and training code.
item.dc:creator: Gabriel Clark, Sofian Mejjoute, George Close, Beren Millidge

item.title: MusicRWKV: A Multimodal RWKV Framework for Music Representation Learning
item.description: arXiv:2611.16718v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Recent music foundation models have achieved remarkable progress in music representation learning, yet most existing approaches rely on Transformer architectures whose quadratic attention complexity introduces substantial computational and memory overhead when modeling long-duration music recordings. In this work, we propose MusicRWKV, a multimodal music representation learning framework built upon the RWKV architecture. MusicRWKV jointly models waveform, spectrogram, and metadata information within a unified self-supervised learning framework. To improve efficiency for long musical sequences, we introduce an invertible compression module that reduces sequence length while preserving reconstruction capability. A FiLM-based conditioning strategy is employed to facilitate modality-aware representation learning without introducing expensive cross-attention operations. We further investigate the integration of Soft ROSA as a differentiable retrieval mechanism for neural-symbolic interaction. Experimental evaluation across a diverse collection of Music Information Retrieval (MIR) benchmarks demonstrates that the proposed RWKV-based architecture can be effectively adapted to heterogeneous music understanding tasks. A controlled pretraining ablation shows that Soft ROSA improves validation performance, while layer-wise telemetry analysis reveals a progressive transition from distributed retrieval to selective retrieval in deeper network layers. These results suggest that RWKV provides a promising architectural alternative to Transformer-based models for multimodal music understanding.
item.dc:creator: Terry Tan

item.title: Convolutional VocalTrax: Replacing Backpropagation Through Time with Convolution in Differentiable Articulatory Synthesis
item.description: arXiv:2611.17181v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: VocalTrax recovers interpretable articulatory controls from a recording by gradient descent through a differentiable Pink Trombone synthesizer. Its vocal tract is a Kelly-Lochbaum waveguide updated twice per audio sample, so every gradient step backpropagates through a long recurrence, which is slow on GPUs. We propose Convolutional VocalTrax, which computes the exact frequency response of the same waveguide and applies it as a causal convolution. We assume that the tract is stationary within 5.8 ms blocks and that its lossy impulse response can be truncated after 93 ms. Gradients then pass through FFTs and a short recursion along the tract instead of through time. On 600 AudioMNIST recordings, the tract forward and backward pass runs 47 to 63 times faster on an A100 GPU, and a classifier trained only on real speech recognizes our reconstructions more often than those of VocalTrax (14.5% vs. 10.0%), although the log-mel distance to the target is 11% higher. Parameters fitted with our model keep this gain when rendered by the original VocalTrax (13.8%).
item.dc:creator: Yongyi Zang, Debasish Ray Mohapatra, Randal Leistikow, Perry R. Cook

item.title: An LLM Is All You Need: Data-Efficient Adaptation to Full-Duplex, Word-Level Spoken Dialogue
item.description: arXiv:2611.14774v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Full-duplex spoken dialogue, in which a system listens while it speaks and can backchannel, yield the floor, and be interrupted, is usually obtained by training on hundreds of thousands to millions of hours of speech. This is costly, rewrites the language model that supplies the system's knowledge, and still leaves turn-taking either implicit or decided coarsely rather than word by word. We show that a frozen, general-purpose multimodal LLM can instead be adapted into a word-level full-duplex system with little data. Our system is a thinker-talker cascade on an 80 ms frame clock. The thinker keeps the LLM frozen and trains only lightweight adapters and a few new token embeddings (97M parameters); at every frame it emits one token of agent text, with pauses, yields, and onsets represented as tokens of the same vocabulary and kept legal by a finite-state machine. A four-stage curriculum, each stage anchored to the model's own behavior under the previous format, performs the conversion in about 30 GPU-hours. The talker reads only the thinker's discrete tokens, so the two halves are trained independently. On Full-Duplex-Bench and InteractionBench, the system is competitive with open-source full-duplex systems built through large-scale speech training: among them, it is the least likely to take the floor when the user merely pauses, backchannels most often, and leads in spoken-task accuracy, groundedness, and coherence over long conversations.
item.dc:creator: Tairan Chen, Richard Yucheng He, Yihang Liu, Baodong Cao, Chen Xu

item.title: Speech Tokenizers are Vulnerable: Transferable Semantic Attack and Robust Tokenizer
item.description: arXiv:2611.14929v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Speech tokenizers serve as speech front ends, encoding input speech signals into representations for downstream models, such as automatic speech recognition (ASR) systems and large audio-language models (LALMs). In this paper, we find that speech tokenizers are fragile at the semantic level: small perturbations can disrupt their semantic encoding process and consequently cause severe degradation in downstream ASR and LALM performance. To study this vulnerability, we propose T-SemAttack, a transferable semantic attack based on a semantic encoder ensemble. By jointly drifting the representation spaces of multiple semantic encoders, T-SemAttack effectively disrupts the semantic content of speech while preserving perceptual quality, thereby inducing error features. We further analyze layer-wise representation drift and cross-model gradient alignment. Our findings show that perturbations can induce substantial shifts in deep semantic representations and that the input gradients of different surrogate encoders exhibit directional alignment. These observations suggest that shared adversarially sensitive directions in the input space may be a key factor underlying cross-model attack transferability. Building on these, we introduce ROSETok, a robust speech tokenizer that combines noisy training with robust semantic distillation to improve reconstruction fidelity and downstream SpeechLLM robustness. Extensive experiments on multiple datasets, 9 open-source and black-box ASR systems, and 4 LALMs demonstrate that T-SemAttack achieves strong transferable attack performance, while the proposed Robust Speech Tokenizer exhibits robustness under high-fidelity reconstruction and downstream tasks. Our code and demo are available at https://wxzyd123.github.io/t-semattack.
item.dc:creator: Zhisheng Zhang, Yifan Mi, Yixuan Zhou, Haiyun Li, Shengbo Cai, Dongfu Song, Ziang Xu, Jie Hao, Zhiyong Wu

item.title: Duo: A Reciprocal World Model for Full-Duplex Interaction
item.description: arXiv:2611.15131v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: In this report, we introduce the Reciprocal World Model (RWM) and present Duo v1, a full-duplex world model that continuously perceives audiovisual inputs while responding to users in real time. The RWM treats intelligence and physical reality as equally fundamental to what constitutes a world. Existing world models largely focus on simulating the latter, leaving reasoning and decision-making as external controls rather than intrinsic parts of the world itself. In RWM, we identify two equally fundamental capabilities: Intent, which provides the cognition underlying world interactions, and Realization, which generates coherent audio-visual behavior. To realize this formulation, Duo v1 introduces three key technical designs: (1) Leveraging autoregressive modeling for continuous interaction reasoning and participation decisions, rather than restricting it to instruction understanding for diffusion models. (2) Constructing chunk-specific conditions and synchronize tokens across Intent and Realization on a unified timeline. Module-specific attention masks enforce causal dependencies both within and across chunks, preventing access to future inputs. (3) Mitigating distribution shift in both modules through dual rollout distillation, training on autoregressively generated Intent tokens and synthesized audiovisual histories from Realization. Both modules continuously perceive real-time audio, video, and text, enabling full-duplex interaction with spontaneous conversations and interruptions. Beyond conversation, users can share real objects, reshape virtual scenes, guide assistants, or play audiovisual games without mouse or keyboard controls. The release of Duo v1 makes our first step, with the next version coming soon. We look forward to broader exploration of this emerging field.
item.dc:creator: Hengyuan Cao, Biao Gong, Guoshan Lu, Qiyuan Zhang, Lin Liu, Yiding Tian, Yilei Jiang, Yuxin Ma, Chengzhang Wu, Kun Chen, Yiqian Xie, Ting Liu, Xin Zheng, Xijun Gu, Tianren Ma, Jiancheng Pan, Chi Zhang, Xuzhe Zheng, Siyi Li, Zhenzhong Lan

item.title: Dynamic Block-Online Streaming ASR for Low-Resource Agglutinative Code-Switching Speech with Morphology-Aware Evaluation
item.description: arXiv:2611.15691v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Low-resource, agglutinative languages challenge low-latency ASR, as fixed lookahead windows fail when grapheme order diverges, suffixes cross code-switch boundaries, or code-switching data is imbalanced. We present the first comprehensive study of streaming ASR for intra-sentential Bangla-English code-switching, identifying a mismatch between strict causal streaming and long-range morphological dependencies. We introduce a Dynamic Block-Online framework with VAD-aligned inference that balances semantics, latency, and context, enabling global bidirectional attention to preserve morphological integrity. To mitigate data scarcity, we propose Script-Anchored Loanword Injection, augmenting training text with English loanwords to model phonotactic transitions. We introduce CS-WER to diagnose switch, root, and suffix errors, and show that flexible latency budgets enhance recognition of agglutinative and mixed-language speech, with successful transfer to menstrual-medical domains.
item.dc:creator: Kazi Rafat, Afifa Imran, Md. Ismail Hossain, Md. Romzan Ali, Fuad Rahman, Sifat Momen, Shafin Rahman, Nabeel Mohammed

item.title: MESH: Multi-receiver Evaluation of Spatial Hearing across Egocentric and Allocentric Views
item.description: arXiv:2611.16787v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Spatial hearing in multi-receiver environments requires identifying who speaks, where they are, and how they move. Existing benchmarks evaluate spatial prediction, transcription, tracking, and distributed speech processing, but offer limited evaluation of whether speech signal remains associated with the correct physical source across receivers and motion. We introduce MESH, which evaluates this association through egocentric and allocentric views of shared acoustic scenes. The egocentric view uses local recordings and peer metadata, while the allocentric view combines synchronized recordings from multiple receivers in a shared 3D world frame. MESH contains nearly 40,000 questions across 13 static and dynamic localization and spatial transcription tasks. We evaluate eleven audio-model configurations and a language-model agent using specialist tools. The best static distance-estimation and dynamic direction-tracking accuracies are only 21.90% and 41.54%, respectively, while the lowest word error rates across four transcription tasks range from 59.15% to 73.10%. Ablation studies and additional experiments reveal that existing models are not yet able to effectively leverage peer information and struggle to handle multi-speaker and dynamic scenarios. These findings highlight the gap between access to distributed acoustic information and its effective use for spatial speech understanding. We release the dataset and evaluation code to support further research on collaborative and distributed spatial hearing.
item.dc:creator: Wen Wen, Bohan Li, KwanHo Tam, Yu Xi, Jing Peng, Shuai Wang, Kai Yu

item.title: Beyond Word Error Rate: A Failure Taxonomy of Streaming Dictation ASR
item.description: arXiv:2611.16919v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Speech recognition (ASR) systems are usually compared by word error rate (WER) on recorded files, after punctuation, capital letters and number format are removed. In dictation, the audio is streamed live and the text goes into the user's message as written, so what matters is which mistakes the user has to fix. The test set, streamed to eleven ASR systems, comprises 106 scripted English dictations from one speaker (read in a quiet room, with a fan on, and whispered), 20 clips in each of eleven other language and dialect sets, and 400 recordings that join clips in two languages. Every error was sorted by a fixed rule into four levels: recognition, output formatting, language handling and, for the self-hosted models, audio dropped before the model. Systems with similar WER failed in different ways. Zoom Scribe and OpenAI's GPT-Live-Transcribe have almost the same WER on quiet English (7.4% and 7.3%), but 34.7% and 8.8% on whispered English. Zoom and both AssemblyAI models left out 26-28% of whispered words, and still 21-26% with their end-of-turn detection relaxed or off; seven other systems left out at most 3%. Qwen3-ASR's 32% came from the speech detection in our own deployment (6% when relaxed). Across 107 EARS speakers, the same four systems lost 7-31% of whispered words, while six others lost under 2%. With only English selected, Gemini, Deepgram and our self-hosted Whisper lost the non-English part of a two-language recording in 86-99% of recordings, against 33-46% with both languages selected, while GPT-Live-Transcribe, OpenAI's realtime Whisper and Meta lost it in at most 20%. Running Whisper behind a Silero voice activity detector that drops audio judged to be silence raised whispered WER from 10.1% to 51.4%. Most English results come from one read speaker. The code, the recordings, both references and every transcript are released.
item.dc:creator: Harras Mansoor, Muhammad Wisal, Hassan Bhatti, Masood Shakir

item.title: Evaluation of Music Version Retrieval Methods for Setlist Identification in Live Concerts
item.description: arXiv:2611.17070v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Automatic setlist identification aims to identify the songs performed in live concert recordings by matching noisy and variable-quality audio against a database of reference tracks. This task presents challenges beyond conventional music version identification, including substantial arrangement differences, background noise, and the need to process continuous recordings efficiently at large scale. In this work, we evaluate modern music version retrieval methods for setlist identification using the ASID benchmark, comparing the established Re-MOVE system with CLEWS and NAVE, an internal neural audio version embedding model. Our results show that NAVE and CLEWS substantially outperform Re-MOVE. Notably, NAVE uses 256-dimensional embeddings, compared with 1024 dimensions for CLEWS, providing a four-fold reduction in embedding storage while achieving better retrieval performance. We further evaluate music/non-music gating and find modest improvements in detection and temporal coverage, while qualitative analysis suggests that such preprocessing can improve recognition boundaries beyond what the standard ASID metrics capture. Overall, the results demonstrate that segment-level audio embeddings provide a strong basis for scalable setlist identification and that compact representations can achieve strong accuracy under realistic live-concert conditions at much lower storage and serving cost.
item.dc:creator: Andres Ferraro, Albin Correya

item.title: Streaming Generation for Music Accompaniment
item.description: arXiv:2510.22105v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Music generation models can produce high-fidelity coherent accompaniment given complete audio input, but are limited to editing and loop-based workflows. We study real-time audio-to-audio accompaniment: as a model hears an input audio stream (e.g., a singer singing), it has to also simultaneously generate in real-time a coherent accompanying stream (e.g., a guitar accompaniment). In this work, we propose a model design considering inevitable system delays in practical deployment with two design variables: future visibility $t_f$, the offset between the output playback time and the latest input time used for conditioning, and output chunk duration $k$, the number of frames emitted per call. We train Transformer decoders across a grid of $(t_f,k)$ and show two consistent trade-offs: increasing effective $t_f$ improves coherence by reducing the recency gap, but requires faster inference to stay within the latency budget; increasing $k$ improves throughput but results in degraded accompaniment due to a reduced update rate. Finally, we observe that naive maximum-likelihood streaming training is insufficient for coherent accompaniment where future context is not available, motivating advanced anticipatory and agentic objectives for live jamming.
item.dc:creator: Yusong Wu, Mason Wang, Heidi Lei, Stephen Brade, Lancelot Blanchard, Shih-Lun Wu, Aaron Courville, Anna Huang

item.title: Optimising Neural Speech Codecs for 300bps Communication using Reinforcement Learning
item.description: arXiv:2605.19541v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: In bandwidth-constrained communication such as satellite and underwater channels, speech must often be transmitted at ultra-low bitrates where intelligibility is the primary objective. At such extreme compression levels, codecs trained with acoustic reconstruction losses tend to allocate bits to perceptual detail, leading to substantial degradation in word error rate (WER). This paper proposes ClariCodec, a neural speech codec operating at 300 bits per second (bps) that reformulates quantisation as a stochastic policy, enabling reinforcement learning (RL)-based optimisation of intelligibility. Specifically, the encoder is fine-tuned using WER-driven rewards while the acoustic reconstruction pipeline remains frozen. Even without RL, ClariCodec achieves 4.64% WER on the LibriSpeech test-clean set at 300 bps, already competitive with codecs operating at higher bitrates. Further RL fine-tuning reduces WER to 3.55% on test-clean, corresponding to a 23.5% relative reduction while preserving perceptual quality. In addition, we adapt ClariCodec to a streaming configuration and show that the proposed RL-based optimisation remains effective under streaming constraints, achieving 4.53% WER on test-clean with a theoretical latency of 374 ms.

item.title: S3-S2ST: Semantically Supervised Streaming Speech-to-Speech Translation
item.description: arXiv:2610.36777v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Streaming speech-to-speech translation requires timely decisions about when partial input is sufficient for accurate translation. We present S3-S2ST, a model that learns to translate and speak from semantically aligned streaming supervision. By converting utterance-level speech pairs into incremental training examples, we teach a learned policy when to commit translations. Its adjustable threshold controls the quality--latency tradeoff on a fixed 640\,ms input grid. S3-S2ST delivers competitive English--Chinese translation on FLEURS and leads the evaluated streaming systems in translation quality on the internal 9-pair test set. On RealSI, adapting the threshold to buffered speech further improves quality over a low fixed threshold with little change in first-audio latency. We have released the training and inference code and 4B model weights at https://github.com/QwenAudio/S3-S2ST

item.title: SonoDyno: A Sonic Dynamometer for Engine Speed and Load Estimation from Audio
item.description: arXiv:2611.06262v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Controllable engine sound synthesis, Active Sound Design and engine order analysis all build on the relationship between the sound of an engine and its momentary operating state: its speed and its load. Recordings of engine sound are abundant in archives, sample packs and online video, yet they rarely carry time-aligned annotations of that state, which limits their applicability to controllable engine sound generation. We present SonoDyno, which estimates the engine speed, the cylinder count and an engine-normalized load intensity from a microphone signal alone, with no tachometer, no bus access and no prior knowledge of the engine configuration. A convolutional scorer of 124,302 parameters reads the energy at the engine orders, the harmonics of half the rotation frequency, in each frame at three time-frequency resolutions to jointly score cylinder count and speed, and a decoder imposes the rotational dynamics of the engine on the speed trajectory. A second head estimates the load intensity, the position of the torque between the engine's drag floor at 0 and its full-load ceiling at 1, from the order levels at the decoded speed. On recordings of engines it has never heard, with microphone position, engine type and cylinder count unknown, SonoDyno places 93 to 97% of the frames within 2% of the true speed, identifies the cylinder count with 80% accuracy and confuses the octave on fewer than 2% of the frames. On an unseen engine of a known type, the load intensity has a mean absolute error of 0.12, and the sign of the torque, driving or braking, is right on 91% of the frames. General pitch trackers fall behind even when the harmonic order of each engine is supplied: on our validation recordings and at a tolerance of 5%, the best of them places 62% of the frames within the tolerance, against 96% for SonoDyno.
